							<h4>Description</h4>
							
							<div style="page-break-after:avoid;"><p>Eparchaean Unconformity - 13° 40′ 0.0012″ N 79°21′0″ E<br><span style="font-size: 1rem;">Natural Arch, Tirumala hills - 13°41′14″N 79°20′25″ E<br></span><span style="font-size: 1rem;">Seshachalam Forests & Sri Venkateswara National Park - 13°45′4″N 79°20′16″ E<br><br></span></p>
<p>The Eparchaean Unconformity in the Tirumala Hills is a geological feature of immense natural and aesthetic significance. The term "Eparchaean Unconformity" refers to a rare and fascinating geological boundary that represents the interface between ancient Precambrian rocks and much younger, overlying geological formations. The Tirumala Hills, located in the Eastern Ghats of Andhra Pradesh, India, offer some stunning landscapes enriched by this geological phenomenon.</p>
<p>The Natural Arch of Tirumala Hills, also known as Silathoranam, is a unique rock formation located near the Tirumala Venkateswara Temple in Andhra Pradesh, India. It is a rare geological wonder and one of the very few natural rock arches in Asia. The arch is believed to be over 1.5 billion years old, naturally formed due to erosion and weathering of quartzite rock. It measures about 8 meters (26 feet) in width and 3 meters (10 feet) in height. The arch is considered sacred by Hindus, as it resembles traditional temple gateways (Thoranam) and is associated with Lord Venkateswara. Located 1 km from the Tirumala temple, the site is a popular attraction for pilgrims and nature enthusiasts. The area surrounding the arch is serene, making it an excellent spot for exploration.</p>
<p>The Tirumala Hills are highlands in Tirupati district of Andhra Pradesh. These hills which are located at approx. elevation of 980 meters above sea level are the seat of remarkable cultural and natural heritage. The Tirumala Hills are considered to be collection of seven peaks of Seshachalam range (which is part of biosphere reserve) of the Eastern Ghats. These hills are namely Seshadri, Neeladri, Garudadri, Anjanadri, Vrushabadri, Narayanadri, and Venkatadri.</p>
<p>These hills have the Eparchaean Unconformity, a major discontinuity of stratigraphic significance that represents a period of remarkable serenity in the geological history of the Earth.<span style="font-size: 1rem;"></span></p></div>
						</div>
					
							<div class="mb-4">
								<h4>Justification of Outstanding Universal Value</h4>
								<div><p>The Eparchaean Unconformity in the Tirumala Hills presents an extraordinary geological contact zone where ancient Archean gneisses, over 2.5 billion years old, visibly meet the younger Proterozoic sedimentary rocks of the Cuddapah Supergroup, capturing a monumental gap in Earth’s geological record and representing one of the most accessible and well-preserved unconformities in the world. This rare phenomenon, designated as a National Geo-heritage Monument, is further enriched by the Natural Arch of Tirumala, one of the few natural rock arches in Asia. Beyond their geological significance, these formations are located within the Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve and Venkateswara National Park, home to diverse and endemic flora and fauna, including the endangered Cycas beddomei and Jerdon’s Courser. The Tirumala Hills embody a rare convergence of ancient Earth history, exceptional natural beauty, ecological richness, and sustained spiritual significance, qualifying it as a site of Outstanding Universal Value. The justification of outstanding universal value is reflected in the following UNESCO listed criteria below.</p>
<p><strong>Criterion (vii):</strong> The Hills of Tirumala with Eparchaean Unconformity, Natural Arch, Hill Forest, and several seasonal waterfalls presents a dramatic combination of monsoon forest of the eastern Ghats of Indian subcontinent.  The area is especially beautiful during rainy season when the hills receive south eastern clouds from Bay of Bengal forming a dramatic Monsson landscape.</p>
<p>The views from the higher elevations of Tirumala offer breath taking panoramas of the surrounding valleys, dotted with temples, forests, and ridgelines. The terrain's dramatic slopes, punctuated by rock outcrops where the unconformity can be studied, creates a visual experience that is both serene and awe-inspiring.</p>
<p><strong>Criterion (viii):</strong> The Eparchaean Unconformity can be seen in exposed rock formations along the hills, where the ancient rocks (dating back over 2.5 billion years) meet the younger strata. The visual contrast between the rugged, timeworn granite and gneiss formations of the older crust and the smoother, sedimentary layers above them creates a striking visual narrative of Earth's geological history. These formations contribute to the area’s unique aesthetic, which marries the rawness of ancient geology with the lush, verdant beauty of the surrounding terrain.</p>
<p>The hills are also seat for Eparchaean Unconformity and exposed in the Ghat section on the way to the sacred Tirumala hills. The unconformity represents initiation of Proterozoic sedimentary basin sedimentation i.e., very first sedimentation over Archean Gneisses. In Cuddapah basin, it is actually represented by Gulcheru Conglomerate, the very first sedimentary unit of Cuddapah Supergroup indicating initiation of the basin sedimentation widely, agreed at~2.0 to 2.1 Ga by different workers (Collins 2015). The feature holds stratigraphic significance representing a period of remarkable serenity in the geological history of the earth. In 2001, the Geological Survey of India (GSI) declared the Eparchaean Unconformity as a National Geo-heritage Monument. It is also well exposed on Kurnool - Nandyal road where 20 m succession of Gulcheru formation unconformably rests on Gadwal Schist Belt. Equally thick Gulcheru Formation is exposed resting over Archean granitic gneisses at Parnapalli on Veldurti- Pulivendla road.</p>
<p>The hills also have Natural Arch, another notified National Geoheritage Monument, which is a distinctive geological feature 1 km (0.6 mi) north of the Tirumala hills temple.</p>
<p><strong>Criterion (x): </strong>Tirumala Hills is part of Venkateswara National Park and Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve. Tirumala hills are one of the most outstanding vegetation zones in Eastern Ghats, with rich floristic diversity, some of them having great medicinal, botanical and economic importance. Several plant species are considered to be endemic to this region (Padmavathi et al., 2012). The Hills are home to rich biodiversity, with tropical forests, endemic flora, and fauna. The presence of ancient geological formations such as the Eparchaean Unconformity enhances the area’s natural beauty by supporting diverse ecosystems. The National Park is known for its many waterfalls and the vegetation in the national park consists of dry deciduous mixed forest with patches of moist deciduous forests in the valleys. The forested slopes are not only picturesque but are vital for the conservation of wildlife, such as the endangered Jerdon’s Courser and other species, making the area not only visually stunning but ecologically significant.</p>
<p>Plants such as South Indian Olibanum <em>Boswellia ovalifoliolata</em>, Beddome's cycas <em>Cycas beddomei</em>, <em>Pimpinella tirupatiensis</em>, Red sandalwood <em>Pterocarpus santalinus</em>, <em>Shorea thumbuggaia, Syzygium alternifolium, Terminalia pallida</em> are endemic to Tirumala hills of seshachalam range falling under the Eastern Ghats of India (Latheef et al., 2008). <em>Cycas beddomei</em>, an endangered species known as the living fossil is endemic to this region (Nethaji et al., 2022).</p>
<p>This biosphere reserve is rich in fauna with 106 species Butterfly species, 7 amphibian species, 34 reptile species and 215 species of birds (Guptha et al., 2012; Guptha et al., 2014, Suryanarayana et al., 2016). Indian golden gecko <em>Calodactylodes aureus</em> an endangered species was rediscovered from hills in this region (Daniel et al., 1986).</p></div>
							</div>
						
							<div class="mb-4">
								<h4>Statements of authenticity and/or integrity</h4>
								<div><p>Two of the geological sites in Tirumala Hills have already been identified as National Geo-heritage Monument. The hills are part of the Venkateswara National Park and covered by densely forested inaccessible areas and thus, preserving the formations.</p>
<p>Eparchaean Unconformity of the Tirumala Hills is not just a geological treasure but also an area of profound aesthetic importance, blending natural beauty, rich biodiversity, and a connection to Earth’s deep history.</p></div>
							</div>
						
							<div class="mb-4">
								<h4>Comparison with other similar properties</h4>
							<p>The Eparchaean Unconformity is an exceptional geological and cultural landmark. This unconformity, first scientifically identified by geologist Robert Bruce Foote in 1872, marks a visible stratigraphic contact between the Archaean granite gneiss (2.5 billion years old) and the Proterozoic sedimentary layers of the Cuddapah Supergroup (1800 to 1400 Million years), thus capturing a significant discontinuity in Earth’s geological history. What makes this site extraordinary is not only its geological clarity and antiquity but also its integration into a rich cultural and spiritual landscape, including the renowned Tirumala temple complex—considered as one of the most sacred pilgrimage destinations in South Asia. It may be compared with other properties inscribed on the World Heritage List that reflect a similar dual heritage.</p>
<strong> </strong>Mountain Resort and its Outlying Temples in Chengde, China<br>
<p>The Mountain Resort and its Outlying Temples in Chengde, China, offers a meaningful parallel. Built between the 18th and 19th centuries, Chengde exemplifies the harmonious integration of imperial palaces and temples with natural landscapes of lakes and forests. Though primarily a cultural site inscribed under Criterion (iv), Chengde’s aesthetic harmony with its natural environment is noteworthy. Similarly, the Eparchaean Unconformity is embedded within the forested, ecologically rich Tirumala Hills and surrounded by temples that have drawn pilgrims for over a millennium. However, unlike Chengde, which is largely man-made, the Eparchaean site foregrounds a vast and ancient natural geological phenomenon that predates human civilization, while simultaneously supporting cultural and spiritual practices rooted in the landscape. Thus, the site transcends the built-natural harmony seen at Chengde by showcasing how natural features themselves become sacred anchors for spiritual identity.</p>
<strong> </strong>Mount Athos, Greece<br>
<p>Mount Athos in Greece offers another parallel. Recognized under Criteria (vi) and (vii), Mount Athos is a sacred spiritual community and a site of outstanding natural beauty, where monastic life has been maintained for centuries in near-complete isolation. Similarly, the Tirumala Hills have functioned for millennia as a sacred refuge and pilgrimage center, where religious practices have continued uninterrupted since ancient times. Both sites demonstrate how rugged, elevated landscapes have served as sanctuaries for spiritual expression and have acquired layered meanings over time. However, while Mount Athos is predominantly a monastic and religious enclave, the Tirumala Hills offer an added dimension: it is a scientifically significant landmark, visibly marking one of the most profound geological discontinuities on Earth.</p>
<p>What makes the Eparchaean Unconformity particularly remarkable among these comparisons is its unique combination of demonstrable geological history and ongoing cultural significance. It visibly captures over a billion years of missing geological record—an outstanding example of deep-time processes that shaped the Indian subcontinent—while continuing to serve as the sacred foundation for one of the most visited pilgrimage destinations in the world. The sacred geography of the Tirumala Hills, encoded in myths, rituals, and temple traditions, is inextricably linked to the physical geography of the site, with the Eparchaean Unconformity forming both a literal and symbolic foundation. This dual narrative—of Earth's ancient evolution and enduring cultural practice—places the Eparchaean Unconformity in a unique position among global heritage sites.</p>
<p>The site may qualify <em>Theme 1: History of planet Earth and evolution of life</em> as per the ‘Geological World Heritage’ (McKeever and Narbonne, 2021) published by IUCN.</p> </div>
